cases.name: AI document assistant with citations
cases.tagline: Retrieval, tenant isolation, citations, evals, and a provider outage plan.
cases.scenario: An internal assistant answers questions over hundreds of thousands of policies, contracts, and support documents for many tenants. A wrong answer is expensive, so every claim needs a source citation. The product must stay useful when the model provider is slow or unavailable.
cases.scale: 500k documents · ~20M chunks · 200 tenants · 50 QPS peak · p95 target under 3 seconds
cases.requirements:
Answers may only use documents the requesting user is allowed to see.
Every material claim should cite a source document and a passage.
Tenant isolation must be enforced before any text reaches the model.
Ingestion must be asynchronous, idempotent, and restartable.
Quality, latency, and token cost must be measured per release.
A provider outage must degrade gracefully, not corrupt data.
cases.constraints:
Documents live in object storage; metadata and permissions live in Postgres.
The model provider has data-retention and regional constraints.
The team is small, so operational surface area matters.
Search quality matters more than supporting every document format on day one.
The system must support evaluation without exposing customer data.
cases.stack:
Django + DRF — API, permissions, run history
PostgreSQL + pgvector — metadata, chunks, vector search (or a dedicated vector DB when scale demands)
Object storage — original documents and extracted text
Worker queue — ingestion, embedding, re-indexing
LLM gateway — provider abstraction, retries, budgets, logging
Observability — traces, latency, token usage, retrieval quality
cases.components:
Document intake and checksum deduplication
Text extraction and structure-aware chunker
Embedding worker with batching and rate limits
Tenant-filtered vector/hybrid retrieval
Reranker and context budgeter
Prompt builder with source blocks and instructions
LLM gateway with timeout, retry, and provider fallback
Citation validator and answer renderer
Evaluation harness with a versioned golden set
cases.data_flow:
User uploads a document; the API stores the original and enqueues ingestion.
The worker extracts text, creates chunks with page/section metadata, and records a version.
Embeddings are generated in batches and stored with tenant/document/chunk references.
A user question is embedded and used for a tenant-filtered vector search.
A reranker selects a small context set that fits the token budget.
The prompt builder labels each passage as untrusted source data.
The LLM gateway calls the model with a timeout and records tokens/latency.
The response is schema-validated, citations are checked against retrieved chunks, and the run is saved.
Unsupported or uncited claims trigger a safe fallback rather than a fabricated answer.
cases.decisions:
Filter by tenant and permissions in the data layer before retrieval; never ask the model to hide documents.
Store page/section spans so citations can be verified, not just hallucinated.
Use asynchronous ingestion with idempotent document/chunk keys.
Put all provider calls behind one gateway with budgets, timeouts, and structured logs.
Gate prompt/model/retrieval changes on an evaluation set and a cost/latency budget.
Keep a safe “I could not find enough evidence” path.
cases.data_model_code:
class Document(TenantScopedModel):
    source_key = models.CharField(max_length=255)
    checksum = models.CharField(max_length=64, db_index=True)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20, default="pending")
    version = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=1)

class Chunk(TenantScopedModel):
    document = models.ForeignKey(Document, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="chunks")
    ordinal = models.PositiveIntegerField()
    text = models.TextField()
    page = models.PositiveIntegerField(null=True, blank=True)
    section = models.CharField(max_length=255, blank=True)
    embedding = VectorField(dimensions=1536)  # pgvector or equivalent

class AnswerRun(TenantScopedModel):
    user = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.PROTECT)
    question = models.TextField()
    prompt_version = models.CharField(max_length=40)
    model_name = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20)  # ok, no_evidence, error
    latency_ms = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=0)
    input_tokens = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=0)
    output_tokens = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=0)

class Citation(models.Model):
    run = models.ForeignKey(AnswerRun, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="citations")
    chunk = models.ForeignKey(Chunk, on_delete=models.PROTECT)
    quote = models.TextField()
cases.starter_code:
def answer_question(tenant, user, question):
    chunks = retrieve_chunks(
        tenant=tenant,
        user=user,
        query=question,
        limit=20,
    )
    selected = rerank_and_fit(chunks, token_budget=6000)
    if not selected:
        return safe_no_evidence_response()

    prompt = build_prompt(
        question=question,
        sources=selected,
        prompt_version="rag-2026-10",
    )
    raw = llm_gateway.generate(
        prompt,
        timeout_seconds=20,
        max_output_tokens=800,
        budget_key=f"tenant:{tenant.pk}",
    )
    answer = validate_answer_schema(raw)
    verified = verify_citations(answer.citations, selected)
    run = AnswerRun.objects.create(
        tenant=tenant,
        user=user,
        question=question,
        prompt_version=prompt.version,
        model_name=raw.model,
        status="ok" if verified else "no_evidence",
        latency_ms=raw.latency_ms,
        input_tokens=raw.input_tokens,
        output_tokens=raw.output_tokens,
    )
    Citation.objects.bulk_create([...])
    return render_grounded_answer(answer, verified)
cases.failure_modes:
Cross-tenant retrieval due to a missing filter.
Stale document version still present in the vector index.
Fabricated citation that looks plausible but is not in the source.
Prompt injection in a retrieved document attempting to change instructions.
Provider timeout or rate limit causing an unbounded retry storm.
Embedding model change silently degrading retrieval quality.
Context stuffed with irrelevant chunks, increasing cost and hallucination risk.
cases.tradeoffs:
Postgres + pgvector is simpler operationally; a dedicated vector store may win at very large scale.
Smaller chunks improve precision but lose context; larger chunks improve context but cost tokens.
Reranking improves quality but adds latency and a second model dependency.
Caching repeated questions saves cost but risks stale or cross-user answers.
Strict citation validation may refuse some correct answers; that is preferable to confident fabrication.
cases.evolution:
Start with one document type, one region, and a measured golden set.
Add hybrid keyword + vector retrieval for identifiers and exact phrases.
Add semantic caching scoped per tenant and invalidated on document changes.
Move embeddings to a dedicated index when ingestion latency or recall targets demand it.
Add model routing for easy queries only after quality is proven per route.
Introduce human feedback loops, but keep evaluation datasets curated and versioned.

cases.name: Tool-using operations agent
cases.tagline: An agent that can act — with scoped tools, approvals, and an audit trail.
cases.scenario: A support operations agent reads tickets, looks up orders, drafts replies, and can issue small refunds. Above a threshold, a human must approve. The agent must never gain ambient database or shell access, and every action needs an attributable record.
cases.scale: 500 support agents · 40k tool calls/day · 3 external systems · strict audit requirements
cases.requirements:
The model proposes tool calls; application code validates and executes them.
Refunds above a configurable threshold require human approval.
Every tool invocation is attributable to a user, run, and policy version.
Read and write permissions are separate and scoped.
Prompt injection from ticket content must not grant new authority.
Operators can disable a tool or the agent immediately.
cases.constraints:
The support platform cannot be rewritten.
External tools have rate limits and inconsistent error formats.
PII must be minimised in prompts and logs.
The agent must remain useful when an approval queue is backlogged.
cases.stack:
Django + DRF — control plane and approval UI
Queue — durable tool jobs and retries
Policy service — limits, roles, tenant scope
Audit store — append-only invocation log
Secrets manager — per-integration credentials
LLM gateway — tool schema and structured output
Read-only mirrors — safe lookups where possible
cases.components:
Agent run orchestrator
Tool registry with JSON schemas and risk levels
Policy engine and approval workflow
Execution sandbox/worker with scoped credentials
Idempotency and deduplication store
Audit and replay UI
Prompt-injection-resistant content handling
Kill switch and per-tenant feature flag
cases.data_flow:
A ticket event creates an AgentRun with a tenant, actor, and policy version.
The model receives a minimal context and a list of allowed tool schemas.
The model proposes a tool call with arguments.
The orchestrator validates the schema, tenant, permissions, and risk policy.
Low-risk reads execute; writes or high-value actions create an ApprovalRequest.
A human approves or rejects with a reason.
The worker executes the approved call with a short-lived scoped credential and idempotency key.
The result is recorded, redacted where required, and returned to the model for the final response.
cases.decisions:
Never let the model execute actions directly; the model only proposes.
Put business limits in code outside the prompt.
Use a separate approval state machine for irreversible actions.
Scope credentials per integration and per tenant, not one global token.
Treat ticket text, attachments, and tool output as untrusted data.
Record enough to replay the decision without storing unnecessary PII.
cases.data_model_code:
class AgentRun(TenantScopedModel):
    actor = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.PROTECT)
    ticket_id = models.CharField(max_length=120)
    policy_version = models.CharField(max_length=40)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20, default="running")
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

class ToolInvocation(models.Model):
    run = models.ForeignKey(AgentRun, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="tools")
    tool_name = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    arguments = models.JSONField()
    risk = models.CharField(max_length=20)  # read, write, irreversible
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20)  # proposed, approved, executed, failed
    idempotency_key = models.CharField(max_length=120, unique=True)
    result_summary = models.JSONField(default=dict)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

class ApprovalRequest(models.Model):
    invocation = models.OneToOneField(ToolInvocation, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    requested_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    decided_by = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, null=True, on_delete=models.PROTECT)
    decision = models.CharField(max_length=20, blank=True)
    reason = models.TextField(blank=True)
    decided_at = models.DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True)
cases.starter_code:
def execute_tool(invocation, actor):
    spec = TOOL_REGISTRY[invocation.tool_name]
    validate_arguments(invocation.arguments, spec.schema)

    policy = Policy.for_tenant(invocation.run.tenant, actor)
    decision = policy.authorize(spec, invocation.arguments)
    if decision.requires_approval:
        ApprovalRequest.objects.get_or_create(invocation=invocation)
        return {"status": "awaiting_approval"}
    if not decision.allowed:
        raise PermissionDenied(decision.reason)

    with scoped_credentials(spec.integration, invocation.run.tenant):
        result = spec.adapter.call(
            invocation.arguments,
            idempotency_key=invocation.idempotency_key,
        )
    invocation.status = "executed"
    invocation.result_summary = redact(result)
    invocation.save(update_fields=["status", "result_summary"])
    return invocation.result_summary
cases.failure_modes:
Prompt injection from a ticket tricks the model into requesting a refund.
Approval is bypassed because the model calls a lower-level write tool.
Retry after timeout issues the same refund twice.
A global integration token exposes every tenant.
Audit logs contain full card numbers or sensitive free text.
A tool outage causes the orchestrator to loop indefinitely.
An operator cannot disable a compromised tool quickly.
cases.tradeoffs:
More approvals reduce risk but increase response time and queue load.
Read-only mirrors are safe but can be stale; direct reads are fresher but broaden access.
Detailed audit logs aid investigations but increase storage and privacy obligations.
A small tool set limits capability but makes the agent easier to reason about and secure.
Autonomy improves throughput but shifts error detection to after the action.
cases.evolution:
Launch read-only tools first and measure accuracy.
Add low-risk writes with strict limits and automatic rollback.
Add approvals and a clear queue only where the business requires them.
Introduce per-tool kill switches and shadow mode.
Move from one general agent to specialised, narrow agents as tasks multiply.
Use evaluation suites for tool selection, argument correctness, and refusal behaviour.

cases.name: Multi-tenant SaaS at scale
cases.tagline: Shared schema, tenant isolation, noisy neighbours, and a path to segmentation.
cases.scenario: A B2B SaaS has thousands of tenants, heavy reporting, and a few enterprise customers whose usage dwarfs everyone else. The product needs strict tenant isolation, predictable performance, and the ability to isolate a large customer later without a rewrite.
cases.scale: 5,000 tenants · 50,000 users · 2 TB Postgres · mixed interactive and batch workloads
cases.requirements:
Every query is tenant-scoped and enforced in the data layer.
Tenant identifiers are never trusted from the client.
Large exports and reports cannot starve interactive traffic.
Billing and usage counters are auditable and idempotent.
A large tenant can be moved to stronger isolation later.
Cross-tenant access is tested and monitored.
cases.constraints:
The team wants one deployable and one primary database initially.
Enterprise contracts require regional data residency.
Reporting queries can scan millions of rows.
The billing provider is external and retries webhooks.
cases.stack:
Django + PostgreSQL — shared-schema tenancy
Redis — cache, rate limits, queue
Worker fleet — exports, reports, notifications
Object storage — exports and attachments
Postgres read replica — reporting where appropriate
Optional row-level security for defence in depth
cases.components:
Tenant resolver and membership middleware
Tenant-scoped manager/query service
Usage metering and quotas
Per-tenant rate limiting and queues
Billing webhook processor
Export/report workers
Cross-tenant audit and anomaly detection
Segmentation/cutover tooling for large tenants
cases.data_flow:
A request authenticates the user and resolves active tenant memberships server-side.
The application sets tenant context for the request and rejects ambiguous access.
Every business query includes tenant_id through a scoped service, not ad-hoc ORM calls.
Write operations include tenant_id in uniqueness constraints and ownership checks.
Expensive reports are queued with per-tenant quotas and produce downloadable artifacts.
Usage events are recorded idempotently and rolled up for billing.
A nightly reconciliation checks counts and tenant boundaries.
cases.decisions:
Use shared schema with tenant_id first for operational simplicity.
Put tenant_id in every tenant-owned table and every relevant unique constraint.
Do not accept tenant_id from request bodies for authorization decisions.
Use per-tenant queues/quotas for heavy work rather than one global FIFO.
Keep a documented path to schema-per-tenant or a dedicated database for enterprise customers.
Treat reporting as a separate workload with its own capacity.
cases.failure_modes:
A missing tenant filter exposes another customer's invoice.
A unique constraint ignores tenant and blocks a legitimate duplicate.
One tenant's export saturates workers for everyone.
Usage events are counted twice after a retry and overbill a customer.
Tenant context leaks into a background task scheduled for another request.
A reporting query locks tables and raises p95 latency for all interactive traffic.
cases.tradeoffs:
Shared schema is cheaper and simpler but relies on scoping discipline.
Schema-per-tenant strengthens isolation but multiplies migrations and connections.
Read replicas help reporting but introduce replication lag.
Per-tenant queues improve fairness but add scheduling complexity.
RLS adds defence in depth but complicates debugging and migrations.
cases.evolution:
Start with shared schema and strict scoped services.
Add per-tenant quotas and export workers before the first enterprise customer.
Introduce a read replica or warehouse for reporting as volume grows.
Add optional RLS for high-risk tables.
Segment enterprise tenants into dedicated schemas/databases when isolation or scale justifies it.
Build cutover tooling and test it on a synthetic large tenant.

cases.name: High-volume webhook and event platform
cases.tagline: Fast acknowledgement, durable deduplication, replay, and backpressure.
cases.scenario: A platform receives signed webhooks from many providers at high volume and must process them into business events. Providers retry aggressively when acknowledgements are slow. Some events arrive out of order, and operations needs a replay tool after a bad deploy.
cases.scale: 10k events/sec burst · 40 providers · 24-hour replay window · strict billing accuracy
cases.requirements:
Acknowledge valid requests quickly and durably.
Deduplicate by provider event ID even across workers.
Process events asynchronously with bounded retries.
Support a safe replay of a time range or failed batch.
Do not lose events if a downstream service is unavailable.
Expose queue lag and failure counts to operators.
cases.constraints:
Providers use different signature schemes and payload shapes.
Some events are only eventually consistent with the provider.
Raw payloads may contain sensitive data and cannot be retained forever.
The team cannot operate a large streaming platform on day one.
cases.stack:
Django API — ingestion and signature verification
Postgres — durable event/outbox state
Queue — workers and retries
Object storage — optional short-lived raw payload archive
Metrics/tracing — per-provider latency and lag
Admin tooling — replay, quarantine, dead-letter review
cases.components:
Ingress endpoint with raw-body verification
Normaliser and provider adapters
Inbound event deduplication table
Business event outbox
Worker pool with concurrency limits
Retry scheduler and dead-letter queue
Replay/quarantine operator tool
Idempotent downstream consumers
cases.data_flow:
Provider sends a signed request; ingress reads the raw body and verifies the signature.
The event is inserted under a unique (provider, event_id) constraint.
If new, a durable job/outbox record is committed; if duplicate, return success.
The worker parses/normalises the payload and applies an idempotent state transition.
Downstream effects are written to an outbox and published with retries.
Failures increment attempts and move to quarantine after a bounded limit.
Operators can replay a filtered set with a new idempotency scope and watch lag.
cases.decisions:
Verify signatures on the raw body before JSON parsing.
Use a database unique constraint for deduplication; do not check-then-insert.
Acknowledge only after the durable event record is committed.
Separate ingestion from business processing with a queue/outbox.
Keep a bounded replay window and redact sensitive payloads after a short period.
Design the consumer to be idempotent, because delivery is at-least-once.
cases.data_model_code:
class InboundEvent(models.Model):
    provider = models.CharField(max_length=40)
    event_id = models.CharField(max_length=160)
    event_type = models.CharField(max_length=120)
    payload_hash = models.CharField(max_length=64)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20, default="received")
    attempts = models.PositiveSmallIntegerField(default=0)
    received_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    processed_at = models.DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True)
    class Meta:
        constraints = [
            models.UniqueConstraint(
                fields=["provider", "event_id"],
                name="unique_provider_event",
            )
        ]
        indexes = [models.Index(fields=["provider", "status", "received_at"])]

class EventOutbox(models.Model):
    topic = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    payload = models.JSONField()
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    published_at = models.DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True)
cases.failure_modes:
Signature verification runs after parsing or on a modified body.
Two workers process the same event because deduplication was a Python check.
A slow downstream call causes provider retries and duplicate load.
A poison event retries forever and blocks a queue partition.
Replay double-applies a non-idempotent effect.
Queue lag grows silently until customer state is hours behind.
cases.tradeoffs:
Persisting every raw payload helps investigations but increases privacy and storage cost.
Strong ordering simplifies consumers but reduces parallelism.
Aggressive retries improve delivery but can amplify an outage.
Immediate synchronous processing simplifies flow but makes providers wait and fail.
A separate event platform adds capability but also operational overhead.
cases.evolution:
Start with Postgres-backed durability and a small worker fleet.
Add per-provider rate limits and backpressure.
Move high-volume streams to a dedicated broker when Postgres or the queue becomes the bottleneck.
Add replay tooling, quarantine dashboards, and automated reconciliation.
Partition by provider/tenant once ordering requirements are explicit.
Track signature failures and duplicate ratios as security/quality signals.

cases.name: Marketplace checkout and ledger
cases.tagline: Money-safe orders, idempotency, stock, refunds, and reconciliation.
cases.scenario: A marketplace processes orders with distinct sellers, platform fees, refunds, and payouts. Customers retry checkout, payment webhooks arrive late, and support occasionally issues manual adjustments. The ledger must explain every balance.
cases.scale: 200k orders/day · multiple currencies · 5,000 sellers · strict financial audit
cases.requirements:
A retried checkout must not create duplicate orders or charges.
Every financial movement is represented in an append-only ledger.
Available stock cannot go negative under concurrent purchases.
Webhook and redirect paths must converge on one order state.
Refunds and manual adjustments are explicit entries, not silent edits.
Seller balances and platform fees are reconcilable to provider data.
cases.constraints:
Payment provider has at-least-once webhooks and its own eventual consistency.
Some orders involve multiple sellers and multiple payouts.
Support needs a safe adjustment workflow with approval.
Historical data includes legacy orders with imperfect fields.
cases.stack:
Django + PostgreSQL — orders, ledger, inventory
Queue — payment reconciliation and payout jobs
Object storage — invoices/exports
Provider API — charges, refunds, payouts
Admin/staff tool — approval-gated adjustments
Metrics — payment success, duplicate rate, ledger imbalance
cases.components:
Checkout/idempotency service
Inventory reservation
Order state machine
Payment intent adapter
Provider webhook processor
Append-only ledger
Refund/adjustment workflow
Payout and reconciliation jobs
cases.data_flow:
Client sends checkout with an idempotency key.
Server creates or returns the existing order and reserves stock atomically.
A payment intent is created with the provider using the same idempotency key.
The redirect and webhook both call one state-transition service.
Ledger entries record charge, fee, refund, and payout movements.
A reconciliation job compares provider records with local ledger entries.
Support adjustments require approval and create compensating entries.
cases.decisions:
Store money in integer minor units with explicit currency.
Use a unique (buyer, idempotency_key) constraint and return the original result on retry.
Model order status as an explicit state machine with guarded transitions.
Never update a balance directly; derive it from append-only ledger entries.
Use one service for provider webhook and redirect reconciliation.
Reconcile against the provider daily and alert on imbalance.
cases.data_model_code:
class Order(models.Model):
    buyer = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.PROTECT)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20, default="pending")
    currency = models.CharField(max_length=3)
    total_cents = models.PositiveIntegerField()
    idempotency_key = models.CharField(max_length=120)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    class Meta:
        constraints = [
            models.UniqueConstraint(
                fields=["buyer", "idempotency_key"],
                name="unique_buyer_idempotency",
            )
        ]

class LedgerEntry(models.Model):
    order = models.ForeignKey(Order, on_delete=models.PROTECT, related_name="ledger")
    kind = models.CharField(max_length=30)  # charge, fee, refund, payout
    amount_cents = models.IntegerField()
    currency = models.CharField(max_length=3)
    provider_ref = models.CharField(max_length=160, blank=True)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    class Meta:
        indexes = [models.Index(fields=["order", "created_at"])]

class SellerBalance(models.Model):
    seller = models.ForeignKey("accounts.Seller", on_delete=models.PROTECT)
    currency = models.CharField(max_length=3)
    available_cents = models.BigIntegerField(default=0)
    pending_cents = models.BigIntegerField(default=0)
cases.starter_code:
@transaction.atomic
def start_checkout(buyer, items, idempotency_key):
    existing = Order.objects.filter(
        buyer=buyer, idempotency_key=idempotency_key
    ).first()
    if existing:
        return existing

    order = Order.objects.create(
        buyer=buyer,
        currency=items.currency,
        total_cents=items.total_cents,
        idempotency_key=idempotency_key,
    )
    for item in items:
        listing = Listing.objects.select_for_update().get(pk=item.listing_id)
        if listing.stock < item.quantity:
            raise ValidationError("Out of stock")
        listing.stock = F("stock") - item.quantity
        listing.save(update_fields=["stock"])
        OrderLine.objects.create(order=order, listing=listing, ...)

    LedgerEntry.objects.create(
        order=order,
        kind="charge",
        amount_cents=order.total_cents,
        currency=order.currency,
    )
    OutboxEvent.objects.create(
        topic="order.created",
        payload={"order_id": order.pk},
    )
    return order
cases.failure_modes:
Payment succeeds but the order remains pending because the webhook was missed.
Two retries create two charges due to a missing unique constraint.
Stock is decremented outside the transaction and oversells.
A refund updates a balance without a ledger entry, breaking reconciliation.
A provider retry is treated as a new order.
A seller payout includes funds that are not yet available.
cases.tradeoffs:
Synchronous payment confirmation gives faster UX but increases coupling and timeout risk.
Holding stock longer reduces oversell but can strand inventory.
A cached balance is fast but must be rebuildable from the ledger.
Multiple currencies add rounding and reporting complexity.
Manual adjustments improve support but require strong approval and audit controls.
cases.evolution:
Start with one currency and one seller per order.
Add a reconciliation job and ledger imbalance alerts before scaling.
Introduce explicit reservations if checkout becomes long-lived.
Partition the ledger by time when it grows large.
Move payouts to a dedicated service when provider complexity grows.
Add fraud/risk checks between checkout and capture, not inside the UI.

cases.name: Real-time notifications at scale
cases.tagline: WebSockets, fan-out, ordering, deduplication, and graceful degradation.
cases.scenario: A product wants live notifications and activity updates for desktop and mobile clients. Some users are highly active, some reconnect constantly, and mobile networks drop connections. The system must remain correct even when real-time delivery fails.
cases.scale: 100k concurrent connections · bursty fan-out · multiple regions · mobile reconnect churn
cases.requirements:
Clients receive new events quickly when connected.
Reconnecting clients can catch up on missed notifications.
Duplicate delivery is possible but must not duplicate user-visible effects.
Presence/online state is advisory, never an authorization signal.
A real-time outage degrades to polling/refresh, not data loss.
Notification permissions and tenant boundaries are enforced server-side.
cases.constraints:
Django app with ASGI for WebSockets.
Redis channel layer for broadcast.
Some clients are behind restrictive networks.
Notification volume spikes during incidents and scheduled events.
The team must operate this without a dedicated real-time platform team.
cases.stack:
Django + Channels — ASGI WebSocket consumers
Redis — channel layer, presence cache, rate limits
PostgreSQL — durable notifications and delivery state
Queue — fan-out and push notification workers
Push providers — APNs/FCM
Load balancer — WebSocket-aware routing
cases.components:
WebSocket authentication handshake
Connection registry and per-user channels
Durable notification table
Fan-out worker
Delivery/dedup tracker
Catch-up API for reconnects
Push notification adapter
Backpressure and rate limiting
cases.data_flow:
Client authenticates and opens a WebSocket with a short-lived ticket.
Server registers the connection and subscribes to user/tenant-scoped groups.
A business event creates a durable Notification row and enqueues fan-out.
The worker publishes to the channel layer for connected users.
The consumer sends the event with a monotonic notification ID.
Client acknowledges; server records delivery if required.
On reconnect, the client requests notifications after its last seen ID.
Push is sent separately for offline users, idempotently.
cases.decisions:
Persist notifications before broadcasting; the socket is not the source of truth.
Use at-least-once delivery plus client/server deduplication by notification ID.
Authenticate the WebSocket and authorize group membership; never trust a client-supplied user ID.
Do not run blocking ORM queries directly in async consumers.
Keep presence out of authorization decisions.
Provide a polling/catch-up fallback for every real-time feature.
cases.starter_code:
async def notification_consumer(scope, receive, send):
    user = scope["user"]
    await send({"type": "websocket.accept"})
    group = f"user-{user.pk}"

    while True:
        message = await receive()
        if message["type"] == "websocket.disconnect":
            break
        # Heartbeat/ack handling; never run blocking ORM here.
        await send({"type": "websocket.send", "text": json.dumps({"type": "pong"})})

# Synchronous worker publishes:
channel_layer.group_send(
    f"user-{notification.user_id}",
    {
        "type": "notification.message",
        "id": notification.pk,
        "payload": notification.payload,
    },
)
cases.failure_modes:
A socket message is treated as delivered when the client was offline.
Clients miss events during reconnect and never catch up.
A broadcast storm consumes workers during an incident.
Presence data is used to authorize access.
Blocking ORM calls freeze the event loop.
Duplicate fan-out sends the same push notification twice.
A client-supplied group name lets one user subscribe to another user's events.
cases.tradeoffs:
WebSockets reduce latency but add stateful connection operations.
At-least-once delivery is simpler than exactly-once but requires deduplication.
Push notifications improve reach but add provider limits and privacy considerations.
A shared channel layer scales horizontally but introduces Redis as a dependency.
Catch-up APIs add query load but are essential for correctness after disconnects.
cases.evolution:
Launch with durable notifications plus polling, then add WebSockets for selected events.
Add catch-up pagination and per-device delivery state.
Introduce push only for offline users and critical events.
Add per-tenant/event rate limits and fan-out quotas.
Partition real-time infrastructure by region when latency requires it.
Measure connection churn, delivery lag, and duplicate rates.

cases.name: Analytics and reporting pipeline
cases.tagline: Keep heavy reporting off the transactional database without lying about the numbers.
cases.scenario: Product and finance teams need dashboards, cohort analysis, and exports over hundreds of millions of events. Running the queries on the OLTP database is slowing checkout. The numbers must be explainable and reproducible.
cases.scale: 100M+ events · 5 years of history · daily and near-real-time dashboards · finance reconciliation
cases.requirements:
Interactive traffic and reporting do not compete for the same database capacity.
Dashboards are reproducible for a stated time window and data version.
Late-arriving and duplicate events are handled explicitly.
Finance totals reconcile with the billing ledger.
Exports are auditable and access-controlled.
Backfills can be rerun without double-counting.
cases.constraints:
The transactional database must remain the source of truth for orders.
Some events arrive hours late from mobile clients.
The team is small; introduce only the infrastructure it can operate.
Historical reports must remain stable even if definitions change later.
cases.stack:
PostgreSQL — OLTP source of truth
Outbox/CDC or scheduled export — movement to warehouse
Columnar warehouse — analytical queries
Django — dashboard API and report orchestration
Object storage — exports and snapshots
Queue — batch jobs and backfills
Metrics — pipeline freshness and row counts
cases.components:
Event collection and validation
Outbox/export worker with idempotent partitions
Warehouse tables/facts and dimensions
Metric definitions/versioning
Dashboard API and caching
Export/report job runner
Data quality checks and freshness alerts
Access control and audit
cases.data_flow:
Business actions write to OLTP and append an outbox/event row.
A scheduled exporter or CDC process moves changes into a warehouse.
Facts are deduplicated by event ID or idempotent partition key.
Transformation models compute daily/hourly metrics with a definition version.
Django serves dashboard queries from warehouse/read models, not OLTP.
Exports are generated asynchronously with a data version and expiry.
A reconciliation job compares finance totals against the ledger.
cases.decisions:
Do not run heavy aggregate queries against the primary OLTP database.
Define metrics as versioned, tested transformations rather than ad-hoc SQL in views.
Make ingestion idempotent by event ID/partition; reruns must not double count.
Handle late events with a watermark or a restatement process.
Separate finance reconciliation from product analytics definitions.
Expose freshness and data version alongside dashboard numbers.
cases.data_model_code:
class AnalyticsEvent(models.Model):
    event_id = models.UUIDField(unique=True)
    event_type = models.CharField(max_length=60)
    tenant_id = models.UUIDField(db_index=True)
    occurred_at = models.DateTimeField(db_index=True)
    received_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    properties = models.JSONField(default=dict)
    schema_version = models.PositiveSmallIntegerField(default=1)

class DailyMetric(models.Model):
    metric = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    tenant_id = models.UUIDField(null=True, blank=True)
    day = models.DateField()
    value = models.DecimalField(max_digits=18, decimal_places=4)
    definition_version = models.CharField(max_length=20)
    computed_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)
    class Meta:
        constraints = [
            models.UniqueConstraint(
                fields=["metric", "tenant_id", "day", "definition_version"],
                name="unique_metric_day_version",
            )
        ]

class ExportRun(models.Model):
    requested_by = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.PROTECT)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20, default="queued")
    filters = models.JSONField()
    data_version = models.CharField(max_length=40, blank=True)
    file = models.FileField(upload_to="exports/%Y/%m/", blank=True)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
cases.starter_code:
def daily_active_users(day, definition_version="v3"):
    cached = DailyMetric.objects.filter(
        metric="daily_active_users",
        tenant_id=None,
        day=day,
        definition_version=definition_version,
    ).first()
    if cached:
        return cached.value

    value = (
        AnalyticsEvent.objects.filter(
            event_type__in=ACTIVITY_EVENTS,
            occurred_at__date=day,
        )
        .values("tenant_id")
        .annotate(users=Count("actor_id", distinct=True))
        .aggregate(total=Sum("users"))["total"] or 0
    )
    DailyMetric.objects.update_or_create(
        metric="daily_active_users",
        tenant_id=None,
        day=day,
        definition_version=definition_version,
        defaults={"value": value},
    )
    return value
cases.failure_modes:
A dashboard query scans the OLTP orders table and slows checkout.
A rerun of a backfill double-counts events because writes are not idempotent.
Late events silently change yesterday's numbers with no restatement marker.
Two teams define “active user” differently and publish contradictory charts.
A schema change breaks the exporter without alerting.
Finance totals do not reconcile with the ledger because both use different cutoffs.
cases.tradeoffs:
Batch ETL is simpler and cheaper but has freshness lag.
Streaming updates are fresher but add operational complexity and duplicate handling.
Pre-aggregated metrics are fast but less flexible; raw event queries are flexible but expensive.
A warehouse adds cost and skills but protects OLTP and enables history.
Denormalized dashboards improve UX but require clear ownership and versioning.
cases.evolution:
Start with a nightly export and a small set of versioned metrics.
Add data quality checks, freshness alerts, and reconciliation with the ledger.
Introduce incremental/CDC loading when volume or freshness demands it.
Add a semantic layer or metric catalog so definitions are shared.
Separate finance-grade reporting from exploratory analytics.
Document restatement policy and show data version in every dashboard.

cases.name: Legacy monolith modernization
cases.tagline: Strangler routing, seams, dual-write risks, and a credible retirement plan.
cases.scenario: A 15-year-old Django monolith still runs the business. Deploys are risky, tests are thin, and the team wants to modernize without a big-bang rewrite. Some modules are tightly coupled to shared tables and cron jobs nobody fully understands.
cases.scale: 1.5M LOC · 6 teams · daily business operations · high cost of downtime
cases.requirements:
Deliver value incrementally without freezing the product roadmap.
Keep the legacy system authoritative until a replacement is proven.
Route capabilities with feature flags and a clear rollback path.
Synchronize data without creating silent divergence.
Make ownership and observability explicit for every extracted capability.
Retire old paths; do not maintain two implementations forever.
cases.constraints:
No complete rewrite is funded.
Some legacy behavior is undocumented and cannot be paused for archaeology.
The database is shared by reports, scripts, and unknown integrations.
Customer-facing downtime is unacceptable during business hours.
cases.stack:
Django monolith — current system
Routing facade / feature flags — gradual cutover
Anti-corruption layer — translate legacy data/contracts
New modular Django apps — extracted capability
Change data capture or outbox — synchronization
Observability — compare old/new outcomes
Dual-write/dual-read ledger — temporary migration safety
cases.components:
Capability inventory and dependency map
Routing facade
Anti-corruption adapters
New module with explicit contracts
Shadow/dual-read comparison
Dual-write or CDC reconciliation
Cutover flags and rollback runbook
Retirement checklist
cases.data_flow:
Inventory a bounded capability and its callers, tables, jobs, and reports.
Put a routing seam in front of the capability.
Run the new implementation in shadow mode on real traffic without side effects.
Compare outputs and error rates; fix discrepancies.
Enable for internal users, then a small cohort, then everyone.
Make the new path authoritative; keep a tested rollback window.
Stop dual writes, migrate remaining readers, archive, and retire the legacy path.
cases.decisions:
Choose a business capability, not a technical layer, as the unit of extraction.
Use a routing facade so callers do not need to know which implementation is active.
Never dual-write without idempotency, reconciliation, and a planned end date.
Keep the database schema compatible during the transition.
Measure parity with real traffic before cutover.
Assign a named owner and retirement criteria for each extracted module.
cases.data_model_code:
class LegacyCapability(models.Model):
    key = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    name = models.CharField(max_length=160)
    owner = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20, default="inventory")
    cutover_percent = models.PositiveSmallIntegerField(default=0)
    retirement_deadline = models.DateField(null=True, blank=True)

class CutoverDecision(models.Model):
    capability = models.ForeignKey(LegacyCapability, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    cohort = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    enabled = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    changed_by = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.PROTECT)
    changed_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    reason = models.TextField(blank=True)

class ParityCheck(models.Model):
    capability = models.ForeignKey(LegacyCapability, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    request_key = models.CharField(max_length=160)
    legacy_result_hash = models.CharField(max_length=64)
    new_result_hash = models.CharField(max_length=64)
    matched = models.BooleanField()
    checked_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
cases.failure_modes:
A big-bang rewrite replaces working behavior with unknown gaps.
Dual writes diverge and nobody notices until a customer complains.
Legacy reports keep reading old tables after the new system becomes authoritative.
A hidden cron job writes to the same data with different rules.
The new path is faster but silently changes business semantics.
Both implementations remain forever because retirement is nobody's job.
cases.tradeoffs:
Incremental modernization is slower in visible scope but reduces catastrophic risk.
Shadow mode consumes extra compute but provides evidence.
Dual writes increase safety but double failure modes and must be temporary.
A routing facade adds indirection but enables gradual cutover and rollback.
Keeping legacy behavior exact may preserve bugs; product decisions must be explicit.
cases.evolution:
Start with a dependency map and one low-risk, high-friction capability.
Add observability and parity checks before enabling any user traffic.
Cut over internal users, then a small cohort, then progressively broader groups.
Decommission dual-write paths and legacy readers on a schedule.
Repeat with the next capability, reusing the routing and comparison tooling.
Use ADRs to record why each legacy behavior is preserved, changed, or removed.
